output.initial_context:
RELEVANT CHARACTER BACKGROUND

Aminata Diallo is a young woman living in a rented room in a crowded district on the outskirts of Bamako, where the housing is basic, with packed-earth walls and a corrugated tin roof, and there is no tap water. Her daily life is defined by early rising, manual labor, long walks, and careful budgeting. She works six days a week on a construction crew as the youngest person there and the only woman. She is physically capable of heavy labor, can haul cement and stack blocks, and is trusted by her master mason, Sékou, to help with load calculations. He calls her la petite comptable because she mentally recalculates measurements before working, and she responds to teasing with quiet nods and verification rather than joking or arguing. Her style is restrained, precise, vigilant, and private.

She values counting, double-checking, and financial caution, habits shaped by poverty and precarious work and by watching her mother lose a market stall after a miscalculated loan. She learned early that spoken plans can be vulnerable, and she tends to keep important plans private. She keeps a small notebook inside her shirt with figures and dates, and she maintains a fixed emergency fund hidden under a loose floorboard near her mattress; the fund is never touched and is not counted in daylight. She does not ask for advances on her wages. She is persistent and disciplined about both work and study, and she makes decisions with close attention to money, timing, distance, and practical constraints.

Aminata is also an accounting student saving for an exam and course at a community center on the other side of the city. Because she cannot afford bus fare both ways, she walks there. She often walks past food stalls without buying in order to save money, and she has declined several social invitations in the past month to preserve time for study and reduce expense. She is saving not only for her course but also for a proper room with running water so her younger sister can live with her and attend school. She does not speak of that plan aloud. Her family history includes her mother’s death when Aminata was twelve and a memory of her father selling his tools to pay for a funeral and then never working as a trowel-holder again. These experiences are part of the background that has made her careful, private, and highly attentive to what can be counted and controlled.

Her relationship with Sékou is significant. Over two years he has taught her the trade and trusted her with calculations. He once lent her a textbook after learning she was studying accounting. His wife has never met Aminata directly but sends greetings through him. Aminata is aware of these connections as part of her work environment and regular social world.

OBJECTIVE SITUATION

After a long day at the construction site, Aminata is packing her trowel when Sékou approaches and invites her to join his family for a large pot of yassa poulet that his wife has prepared for the neighborhood’s Korité celebration tonight. Aminata is exhausted. She had planned to study for her accounting exam by lamplight. She knows that declining a meal invitation during Korité can seem rude. She also knows that accepting would involve spending money on a bus fare across town and time away from her books. She must decide whether to accept or politely decline.

PRE-APPRAISAL STATE AND ACCESSIBLE MEMORIES

Aminata is physically worn down: her shoulders ache from hauling cement, her right hand is blistered where the trowel handle rubbed, and she has not eaten since a piece of bread at dawn. Her exam notes are tucked inside her shirt and are damp with sweat. She is in the immediate aftermath of a full workday and is still in work clothes and work routine, with study materials on her person.

The smell of yassa poulet directly calls up an earlier Korité meal before her mother died, when they ate together at a neighbor’s table. Sékou’s phrase that his wife has prepared the meal echoes the way her mother used to announce food. These cues are accessible from the present situation and are linked to family, shared meals, and Korité, without adding reflective interpretation.
